newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Young Asians not consumed by materialism - survey.
newsitem.headline: Young Asians not consumed by materialism - survey.

text.p: Young Asians are not driven purely by materialism and continue to treasure traditional values of hard work, humility and family ties, according to a survey released on Wednesday.

The survey by advertising agency Ogilvy & Mather Asia Pacific (O&M) found young Asians differ vastly from their Western counterparts in seeking to engage in society while asserting independence of thought and self-expression.

"They desire a kind of controlled freedom in which they carry forward much of their Asian heritage, for example respecting their elders and authority," Mark Blair, O&M's regional planning director, told a news conference.
O&M is part of Britain's WPP Group Plc.
The survey included 7,000 individual interviews and 66 extended group discussions with the urban, educated elite aged 20 to 30 in 14 cities in Southeast Asia, China and India.

It also covered interviews with 27 "trend gurus" in these markets, including editors of national newspapers and fashion magazines, disc and video jockeys, and sociology professors, which provided insights for some of the survey questions.

Identifying its target group as the Generation who Independently Engage (Genie), the survey drew distinctions between young people in Asia and their Western counterparts, often described as the disenfranchised Generation X.
It found that rather than feeling isolated from society, young Asians recognise the opportunities society offers them and are essentially optimistic about their prospects in life.

"The Genie are given the opportunity to realise their ambitions, whereas in the West, young people are facing intense depression about the lack of opportunities due to economic recession," Blair said.
The survey also found that Asians take a very pragmatic approach to money, seeing it as a means to buy their way to the top of the ladder.
"Unlike the sense of shame over being middle class in the West, young middle class Asians see themselves as part of a corpus driving Asia," he said.
The survey found that young people in India were most likely to move to a higher paying job despite having no complaints with their current job, while those in Hong Kong were least likely.
Filipinos gave education more importance than any of their counterparts, while Singaporeans were the most likely to reject the importance of saving for the future.
Young people in China were the most keen to emigrate to the West for a period of time if an opportunity arose, whereas those in Taiwan felt most strongly about their political rights.

Blair said the findings of the more than US$500,000 survey were important for advertisers because they show a superficial adoption of Western fashions among Asia's youth did not necessarily imply like-mindedness.
"People are beginning to appreciate how important it is to get communication right for the Asian community because of the size of this market," he said.
Advertisers in Asia tended to focus mainly on promoting the quality of a product and the status it conferred on its users, said John O'Shea, group managing director of O&M, Singapore.

He said there were largely untapped opportunities for advertisers to highlight the other roles that a brand played, including offering a means of self-expression or a reward for coping with the pressures of urban life.
